c.tagline: Where the Great Wall meets the sea and Beijing goes to the beach.

taxi.fareNote: Metered from about ¥8; summer beach-season demand in Beidaihe can mean waits and negotiated flat rates. Pay by Alipay/WeChat or cash.

emergency.note: 110 reaches police, 120 an ambulance, and 119 the fire service; there is no single combined emergency number, and 112 works from mobiles to route you.

hood_landmark.Gold Coast (Beidaihe New District): Gold Coast sand dunes, Changli, Qinhuangdao

avoid.reason: Expect vendor overcharging and tout pressure at Beidaihe and Nandaihe beaches in summer; agree on prices first.

hood_desc: Qinhuangdao's downtown port district and its economic and administrative core, with the main railway station, shopping streets, and the Olympic Sports Center; the practical, year-round base with the best transport links.

China's most famous seaside summer resort, a leafy district of sandy beaches, sanatoriums, and villas that fills with holidaymakers from Beijing and Tianjin each summer; the place to stay for the beach and Pigeon Nest Park sunrise views.

The walled Ming garrison town where the Great Wall meets the sea, home to the 'First Pass Under Heaven' gate and Old Dragon's Head (Laolongtou); Qinhuangdao's headline history and its most sightseeing-rich quarter.
A quieter beach-resort strip just south of Beidaihe with wide sands, water parks, and the Nandaihe International Entertainment Center; a calmer, family-friendly alternative to busy Beidaihe.

The Gold Coast (Huangjin Hai'an) dunes and Beidaihe New District to the south, known for China's tallest coastal sand dunes, birdwatching wetlands, and newer resorts; a spread-out, nature-focused area.

Beidaihe Yijing Tiger Stone Marine Park Hotel

water.note: Drink bottled or boiled water, as everywhere in mainland China.

transit.hours: City buses run roughly 5:30 AM to 9:30 PM, with extra tourist lines in the summer season; there is no metro.
transit.note: Qinhuangdao has no metro; city buses link the port district (Haigang) with the Beidaihe beaches and Shanhaiguan, supplemented by taxis, DiDi, and seasonal tourist shuttles in summer.
transit.pay: Pay by scanning an Alipay or WeChat Pay QR code, tapping a rechargeable transit card, or cash (exact change, flat ¥1-2 fare) on board.

bus: Coaches to Beidaihe, Shanhaiguan, and across Hebei

car.idp: Not valid — China does not recognize the International Driving Permit; a temporary Chinese driving permit is required to drive.

ferry: Qinhuangdao Port and seasonal passenger boats on the Bohai Sea
train: Qinhuangdao Railway Station and Beidaihe Station (Beijing–Harbin and Beijing–Shenyang high-speed rail)

transit.m: Airport shuttle bus to Beidaihe / Qinhuangdao downtown (~40 min)
Taxi to the city center (20-30 min)

tip.r: Tipping is not customary or expected in China; no service charge or gratuity is needed at restaurants, hotels, or taxis.

food.name: Beidaihe Steamed Seafood
food.desc: The Bohai Sea catch cooked simply - steamed jiaji fish, quick-fried whelk, salted prawns and fried crab, ordered by pointing at the tanks.

places.name: Fishman Dock (Yu Ma Tou)
places.note: The city's biggest seafood house, known for steamed jiaji fish and fried crab straight off the boats.

places.name: Lao Bai Mao Seafood
places.note: Long-running Beidaihe seafood restaurant that locals name first for a summer sea feast.

places.name: Liuzhuang Seafood Market
places.note: Buy the catch at the market and pay a nearby kitchen to cook it - the local way.

food.name: Grilled Oysters
food.desc: Bohai oysters split on the shell and grilled with garlic, chilli and glass noodles until bubbling - the signature snack of Beidaihe summer nights.

places.name: Baoshu Seafood Barbecue
places.note: Grill house known for garlic oysters and skewered seafood cooked over charcoal.

places.name: Liuzhuang night market
places.note: Beidaihe's best-known evening food street, wall-to-wall oyster and squid grills in season.

places.name: Beidaihe beachfront stalls
places.note: Open-air stalls along the beach road grill oysters to order until late.

food.name: Mackerel and Chive Dumplings
food.desc: Bayu jiaozi - minced Spanish mackerel with pork fat and chives, folded into thin skins and boiled; a Bohai coast speciality you won't find inland.

places.name: Wanghai Seafood
places.note: Sea-themed local eatery whose seafood dumplings are a standing order with regulars.

places.name: Fishman Dock (Yu Ma Tou)
places.note: Serves mackerel dumplings alongside the seafood menu - a good place to try them fresh.

places.name: Shanhaiguan Ancient City food street
places.note: Dumpling shops along the old-town street boil seafood and pork jiaozi all day.

food.name: Sitiao Baozi
food.desc: Shanhaiguan's century-old steamed buns, pleated into four long ridges and filled with seasoned pork - eaten with vinegar and raw garlic.

places.name: Sitiao Baozi Pu
places.note: The original Shanhaiguan bun shop, a local institution since the Qing era.

places.name: Shanhaiguan Ancient City food street
places.note: Several bun houses near the First Pass under Heaven gate steam them all morning.

places.name: Shanhaiguan old-town breakfast stalls
places.note: Cheap early-morning stalls pair the buns with soy milk and pickles.

food.name: Hun Guo Hotpot
food.desc: Shanhaiguan's winter hotpot: a copper pot layered with pickled cabbage, pork belly, blood sausage, tofu and prawns, simmered over charcoal at the table.

places.name: Shanhaiguan Ancient City restaurants
places.note: Old-town kitchens run hun guo through the cold months; the classic post-Great Wall meal.

places.name: Fishman Dock (Yu Ma Tou)
places.note: Large local restaurant that adds seafood to the traditional northeastern hotpot.

places.name: Baoshu Seafood Barbecue
places.note: Warm indoor option pairing hotpot-style stews with charcoal seafood in winter.

food.name: Sesame-Paste Malatang Noodles
food.desc: Qinhuangdao's own take on malatang - skewers and noodles cooked in broth then drowned in thick sesame paste rather than chilli oil.

places.name: Lao Er Wei
places.note: The city's famous sesame-paste malatang shop; queues out the door at lunchtime.

places.name: Liuzhuang night market
places.note: Night-market stalls serve the local sesame-paste style alongside grilled seafood.

places.name: Shanhaiguan Ancient City food street
places.note: Noodle and malatang counters aimed at locals rather than tour groups.

food.name: Changli Red Wine
food.desc: Qinhuangdao's Changli County is one of China's oldest wine regions, planting Cabernet on the coastal hills since the 1980s.

places.name: Chateau Huaxia
places.note: Pioneer Changli estate with cellar tours and tastings of its dry reds.

places.name: Bodega Langes
places.note: Austrian-founded winery on the Changli slopes, open for tasting visits.

places.name: Fishman Dock (Yu Ma Tou)
places.note: Stocks Changli bottles, the easy way to try the local wine with seafood.

food.name: Fresh Draft Beer
food.desc: Zha pi - unpasteurised draught beer sold by the plastic bag or jug from neighbourhood taps, the standard partner to grilled oysters.

places.name: Liuzhuang night market
places.note: Draft beer poured by the jug at every grill stall through the summer season.

places.name: Bilata Sea Bar Park
places.note: Seaside bar park where the beer comes with live music and sea views.

places.name: Baoshu Seafood Barbecue
places.note: Cold draught by the pitcher alongside the charcoal grill.

landmarks: Shanhaiguan (First Pass Under Heaven)
The mighty walled fortress where the Great Wall meets the eastern plains, its gate tower bearing the famous inscription First Pass Under Heaven.
Laolongtou (Old Dragon's Head)
The dramatic terminus where the Great Wall marches straight into the Bohai Sea, its stone dragon-head rampart lashed by waves.
Jiaoshan Great Wall
The first mountain section of the Great Wall, climbing steeply from Shanhaiguan with restored watchtowers and panoramic sea-and-summit views.
Mengjiangnü Temple
A hillside shrine to the legendary weeping widow whose tears collapsed the Great Wall, a beloved site of Chinese folklore since the Song dynasty.
Beidaihe Beach
China's most storied seaside resort, a long golden strand of gentle surf where emperors, leaders and holidaymakers have summered for over a century.
Pigeon Nest Park (Gezhenwo)
A rocky headland in Beidaihe famed as the finest place in northern China to photograph the sun rising over the Bohai Sea.
Beidaihe Wetlands and Bird Sanctuary
Expansive coastal marshes on a major East Asian flyway, drawing birdwatchers worldwide for cranes, spoonbills and hundreds of migratory species.
Qinhuangdao Wildlife Park
A vast forested safari park near Beidaihe where visitors ride through open enclosures of tigers, bears and herds of deer.
Xin'ao Undersea World
A popular Beidaihe aquarium with a walk-through shark tunnel, beluga shows and exhibits of Bohai and tropical marine life.
Qinhuang Qiuxian Ruhai Chu (Emperor Qin's Departure Point)
A seaside park commemorating the spot where China's first emperor reputedly dispatched expeditions to seek the elixir of immortality.

train.note: Qinhuangdao has no international trains. Most visitors arrive from Beijing or Tianjin, and the Beijing-Harbin high-speed line puts Beijing roughly two to two and a half hours away, with Beidaihe station the more convenient stop for the beaches and Shanhaiguan station the one for the Great Wall's eastern end at Old Dragon's Head. The city is on the main corridor to the northeast, so there are also through trains to Shenyang, Changchun and Harbin. Book on 12306 with your passport, and note that summer weekends to Beidaihe sell out quickly as this is Beijing's traditional seaside resort.

bus.note: There are no international coaches. Long-distance buses use the central station near the main train station in the Haiguan area, running to Beijing, Tianjin, Tangshan, Shenyang and towns across eastern Hebei. Journey times to Beijing are around four hours against roughly two by high-speed train, so the coach is only worth it for places the railway misses.

ferry.note: Qinhuangdao is a working port but its harbour is overwhelmingly a bulk coal and cargo terminal rather than a passenger one, and there are no scheduled passenger ferry sailings; the only boats for visitors are short pleasure cruises off the Beidaihe and Nandaihe beaches in summer.

full.name: Tangshan
full.blurb: An industrial city about two hours west rebuilt after a devastating 1976 earthquake and now has a memorial park documenting the disaster.

full.name: Chengde
full.blurb: The Qing dynasty's mountain summer resort and surrounding temples lie roughly three and a half hours northwest, built to host Tibetan and Mongolian dignitaries.

full.name: Beijing
full.blurb: China's capital is reachable by high-speed rail in about two and a half hours, with imperial palaces, temples, and museums filling a full day.
